Get started

Source: vignettes/OccurrenceCleaner.Rmd
OccurrenceCleaner.Rmd

This article flags a small set of species records, removes the records a chosen cleaning rule flags, and counts what two different rules exclude. It assumes basic R and data frames. The coordinate tests follow CoordinateCleaner (Zizka et al. 2019), with the same definitions and default distances. The documented differences are listed in Where the flags differ.

  1. Flag the records with flag_occurrences().

  2. Inspect the flags with print() and summary().

  3. Filter out flagged records, using keep_unflagged().

  4. Compare rules with tally_flags().

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/OccurrenceCleaner")

Needs a C++ compiler; Installation shows how to set one up.

Flagging a data frame

The example has seven records of four tree species, each with an identifier. Coordinates are longitude and latitude in decimal degrees. The column names follow Darwin Core, the standard set of field names for biodiversity data.

library(OccurrenceCleaner)

x <- data.frame(
  id = 1:7,
  species = c("Quercus robur", "Quercus robur", "Fagus sylvatica",
              "Fagus sylvatica", "Pinus nigra", "Pinus nigra",
              "Picea abies"),
  decimalLongitude = c(14.05, 0, 16.37, 16.37, 200, -30, 13.06),
  decimalLatitude = c(47.85, 0, 48.21, 48.21, 45, 40, 47.08)
)

flag_occurrences() runs the tests named in tests. The first three need no reference data:

  • invalid: a coordinate is missing, not numeric, or outside the range of longitude and latitude.

  • zero: longitude or latitude is exactly zero, or the point lies within 0.5 degrees of (0, 0).

  • duplicate: the record has the same species and coordinates as an earlier record.

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "zero", "duplicate"))
f
#> <occ_flags> 7 records, 3 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#>   id         species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude flags flagged_by
#> 1  1   Quercus robur            14.05           47.85     0           
#> 2  2   Quercus robur             0.00            0.00     2       zero
#> 3  3 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21     0           
#> 4  4 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21  1024  duplicate
#> 5  5     Pinus nigra           200.00           45.00     1    invalid
#> 6  6     Pinus nigra           -30.00           40.00     0           
#> 7  7     Picea abies            13.06           47.08     0

The result is x with the same rows in the same order and its columns unchanged, plus the flag columns described below. The printed display also shows a flagged_by column naming the tests that flag each record; the object itself has no such column. Record 2 has zero coordinates, record 4 repeats record 3, and record 5 has a longitude of 200 degrees.

A record without a flag has passed only the tests that were run. Record 3 lies in Vienna but carries no flag, because no test against capitals has run yet.

Each test also has a logical column, flag_<test>, which is TRUE where the test flagged the record. The flags column combines the results of all tests for a record into one integer; The tests in detail explains the encoding.

f$flag_duplicate
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE

Filtering records

A cleaning rule is the set of tests whose flags exclude a record. keep_unflagged() keeps the records that no test in the rule flags. It also checks that every named test was run on the flagged table, and stops with an error if one was not:

rule <- c("invalid", "zero", "duplicate")
cleaned <- keep_unflagged(f, rule)
cleaned[, c("id", "species", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")]
#>   id         species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
#> 1  1   Quercus robur            14.05           47.85
#> 3  3 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21
#> 6  6     Pinus nigra           -30.00           40.00
#> 7  7     Picea abies            13.06           47.08

Record 3 is kept and record 4 is excluded: the duplicate test flags only the repeats, so one copy of each record remains.

Running every test the columns allow

Without tests, flag_occurrences() runs every test whose columns are in the data. Running a test only adds its flags, so the default checks for every potential problem the columns allow. Which records to exclude is a separate choice, made afterwards with a cleaning rule.

With coordinates and species, the default adds tests against reference points and polygons: country capitals, country centroids, biodiversity institutions, the headquarters of the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), urban areas, the land, and the Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023), a list of coordinates that recur in GBIF records for reasons such as georeferencing defaults. It also runs the test for geographic outliers within a species. The printed header names the columns whose tests could not run, such as a country code or GBIF’s reported issues, and test_plan() lists those tests with the reason for each.

f <- flag_occurrences(x)
f
#> <occ_flags> 7 records, 12 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#> # not run, missing input: countryCode, issue, basisOfRecord, establishmentMeans, min_ma, max_ma, datasetKey, range polygons, genus (18 tests); test_plan() lists them
#>   id         species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude     flags
#> 1  1   Quercus robur            14.05           47.85         0
#> 2  2   Quercus robur             0.00            0.00 134217862
#> 3  3 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21       264
#> 4  4 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21      1288
#> 5  5     Pinus nigra           200.00           45.00         1
#> 6  6     Pinus nigra           -30.00           40.00       128
#> 7  7     Picea abies            13.06           47.08         0
#>                flagged_by
#> 1                        
#> 2     zero,equal,sea,aohi
#> 3           capital,urban
#> 4 capital,urban,duplicate
#> 5                 invalid
#> 6                     sea
#> 7

Records 3 and 4 lie in Vienna, within 10 km of a capital and inside an urban area. Record 6 is in the Atlantic. Record 2, at (0, 0), is also at sea, has equal longitude and latitude, and lies within 10 km of an inventory point. The outlier test flags no record. Records 1 and 7 pass every test run here.

The sea test compares each record with land polygons from Natural Earth, at the 1:110 million scale by default. Near coasts and on small islands a finer scale (land_scale = 50 or 10) can change the flag; Reference data maps the difference.

A flagged record may still be valid: a beech can grow within 10 km of a capital, so you decide which tests suit your analysis. A rule for species distribution modelling might exclude fossil and living specimens along with coordinate problems, and another study can choose a different set.

summary() counts the records each test flags, and in the only column the records that test alone flags. Without a rule, it counts under one rule named all that lists every test that was run. It only counts: f still contains all seven records.

summary(f)
#> <occ_summary> 7 records
#>   rule all: removes 5 (71.43 %)
#>  rule              test n flagged   pct only pct_only
#>   all           invalid 7       1 14.29    1    14.29
#>   all              zero 7       1 14.29    0     0.00
#>   all             equal 7       1 14.29    0     0.00
#>   all           capital 7       2 28.57    0     0.00
#>   all          centroid 7       0  0.00    0     0.00
#>   all       institution 7       0  0.00    0     0.00
#>   all gbif_headquarters 7       0  0.00    0     0.00
#>   all               sea 7       2 28.57    1    14.29
#>   all             urban 7       2 28.57    0     0.00
#>   all         duplicate 7       1 14.29    0     0.00
#>   all           outlier 7       0  0.00    0     0.00
#>   all              aohi 7       1 14.29    0     0.00
#>   all             (any) 7       5 71.43

A rule excludes each record once, however many of its tests flag it. Record 2 is flagged by four tests and record 4 by three, so the per-test counts add up to 11 while the (any) row excludes 5 records.

Comparing cleaning rules

Several rules can be compared on the same flags without running the tests again. Here the strict rule adds the capital and sea tests to the mild one. tally_flags() counts, per species, the records each rule removes:

strict <- c("invalid", "zero", "capital", "sea", "duplicate")
mild <- c("invalid", "zero", "duplicate")
t <- tally_flags(f, by = "species",
                 rules = list(strict = strict, mild = mild))
t
#> <occ_tally> 7 records in 4 groups of species, rules: strict, mild
#>          species n removed_strict kept_strict removed_mild kept_mild
#>  Fagus sylvatica 2              2           0            1         1
#>      Picea abies 1              0           1            0         1
#>      Pinus nigra 2              2           0            1         1
#>    Quercus robur 2              1           1            1         1
#> # summary() for the share each test flags

Under the strict rule both beech records go; under the mild rule one stays. tally_flags() also cuts numeric columns such as the record year into bins, which Choosing a cleaning rule shows.

Changing a test’s distance

The distances are part of the tests, so changing one means flagging again. The capital test flags records within 10 km of a capital by default. With 200 m, the Vienna records pass it:

f200 <- flag_occurrences(x, buffers = list(capital = 200))
f200[3:4, ]
#> <occ_flags> 2 records, 12 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#> # not run, missing input: countryCode, issue, basisOfRecord, establishmentMeans, min_ma, max_ma, datasetKey, range polygons, genus (18 tests); test_plan() lists them
#>   id         species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude flags      flagged_by
#> 1  3 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21   256           urban
#> 2  4 Fagus sylvatica            16.37           48.21  1280 urban,duplicate

The capital distance is given in metres, as are the other proximity distances; the zero distance is in degrees. The help page of flag_occurrences() lists the default of each test.

Flagging other data

Other data usually arrives as a file with its own column names. The example below writes the records to a CSV file with the columns taxon, lon and lat, then reads it back as any CSV file would be read:

csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(taxon = x$species, lon = x$decimalLongitude,
                     lat = x$decimalLatitude),
          csv, row.names = FALSE)
y <- read.csv(csv)

Columns are found by their Darwin Core names regardless of capitalisation. Other names are set with occ_columns(), and for another file only the read.csv() path and these names change:

cols <- occ_columns(lon = "lon", lat = "lat", species = "taxon")
flag_occurrences(y, columns = cols)
#> <occ_flags> 7 records, 12 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#> # not run, missing input: countryCode, issue, basisOfRecord, establishmentMeans, min_ma, max_ma, datasetKey, range polygons, genus (18 tests); test_plan() lists them
#>             taxon    lon   lat     flags              flagged_by
#> 1   Quercus robur  14.05 47.85         0                        
#> 2   Quercus robur   0.00  0.00 134217862     zero,equal,sea,aohi
#> 3 Fagus sylvatica  16.37 48.21       264           capital,urban
#> 4 Fagus sylvatica  16.37 48.21      1288 capital,urban,duplicate
#> 5     Pinus nigra 200.00 45.00         1                 invalid
#> 6     Pinus nigra -30.00 40.00       128                     sea
#> 7     Picea abies  13.06 47.08         0

With the three columns mapped, the same 12 tests run as on x.

Fixing common errors

Data often use other column names than the Darwin Core ones. In this example, y stores the coordinates as lon and lat and the species as taxon. The columns argument tells OccurrenceCleaner which columns to read.

Running the tests without that mapping produces this error:

flag_occurrences(y)
#> Error in `apply_plan()`:
#> ! no test can run on this input: no column `decimalLongitude` and `decimalLatitude` for the coordinates, nor another column a test reads; name the columns with occ_columns(), and see test_plan() for what each test needs

The message names the coordinate columns it looked for and points to occ_columns(). Passing the mapping cols from Flagging other data fixes the call:

fy <- flag_occurrences(y, columns = cols)
print(fy, n = 3)
#> <occ_flags> 7 records, 12 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#> # not run, missing input: countryCode, issue, basisOfRecord, establishmentMeans, min_ma, max_ma, datasetKey, range polygons, genus (18 tests); test_plan() lists them
#>             taxon   lon   lat     flags          flagged_by
#> 1   Quercus robur 14.05 47.85         0                    
#> 2   Quercus robur  0.00  0.00 134217862 zero,equal,sea,aohi
#> 3 Fagus sylvatica 16.37 48.21       264       capital,urban
#> # ... 4 more records; summary() for the share each test flags

A mapping that leaves out a column gives no error: the tests that need that column do not run. Here the species column is left out:

cols_xy <- occ_columns(lon = "lon", lat = "lat")
print(flag_occurrences(y, columns = cols_xy), n = 3)
#> <occ_flags> 7 records, 10 tests, reference OccurrenceCleaner 0.2.0, land 110
#> # not run, missing input: countryCode, species, issue, basisOfRecord, establishmentMeans, min_ma, max_ma, datasetKey, genus (20 tests); test_plan() lists them
#>             taxon   lon   lat     flags          flagged_by
#> 1   Quercus robur 14.05 47.85         0                    
#> 2   Quercus robur  0.00  0.00 134217862 zero,equal,sea,aohi
#> 3 Fagus sylvatica 16.37 48.21       264       capital,urban
#> # ... 4 more records; summary() for the share each test flags

The header counts 10 tests instead of 12 and lists species among the missing inputs: the duplicate and outlier tests did not run. Adding species = "taxon", as in cols, runs them again.

An unknown test name stops the call before any test runs:

flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capitals")
#> Error in `check_tests()`:
#> ! unknown test(s): capitals. See flag_tests().

flag_tests() lists the valid names; the capital test is called capital:

fc <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")
fc$flag_capital
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE

A rule that names a test which was not run also stops with an error, because the rule would otherwise exclude no records for that test:

f3 <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "zero"))
has_flag(f3, c("zero", "sea"))
#> Error in `check_tests_run()`:
#> ! test(s) not run on these flags: sea; run flag_occurrences() with them, or drop them from the rule

The fix is to run flag_occurrences() with the test, or to drop it from the rule. Here the sea test is added:

f3 <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "zero", "sea"))
has_flag(f3, c("zero", "sea"))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

Checks based on GBIF metadata

Some tests read GBIF fields instead of the coordinates. basis_fossil flags records whose basis of record is a fossil specimen. The example adds a basisOfRecord column to a copy of the records, xb, and marks record 7 as a fossil:

basis <- c(rep("HUMAN_OBSERVATION", 6), "FOSSIL_SPECIMEN")
xb <- data.frame(x, basisOfRecord = basis)
fb <- flag_occurrences(xb, tests = "basis_fossil")
fb$flag_basis_fossil
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

Cleaning GBIF data uses these tests on a GBIF download, including the issue warnings and establishment means.

Flagging a table on disk

flag_occurrences() also takes a path to a table on disk, such as the directory of Parquet files of a GBIF snapshot. Each file is flagged and written separately to out, and keep names the input columns copied next to the flags.

The example writes the seven records to a directory src as two files. The files use the .vtr format of vectra, the column-store package OccurrenceCleaner reads and writes tables on disk with:

src <- tempfile("records")
dir.create(src)
vectra::write_vtr(x[1:4, ], file.path(src, "part-1.vtr"))
vectra::write_vtr(x[5:7, ], file.path(src, "part-2.vtr"))

The call is the same as for a data frame, with the path and an output directory. The identifier is looked for under its GBIF name gbifID by default, so columns maps it to id:

out <- flag_occurrences(src, out = tempfile("flags"),
                        columns = occ_columns(id = "id"),
                        keep = "species", verbose = FALSE)

For a path, the result describes the output directory instead of holding the records. The directory’s files hold the identifier, the keep columns and the flags of every record. tally_flags() reads the directory like a data frame:

t <- tally_flags(out, by = "species", rules = list(strict = strict))
t
#> <occ_tally> 7 records in 4 groups of species, rules: strict
#>          species n removed_strict kept_strict
#>  Fagus sylvatica 2              2           0
#>      Picea abies 1              0           1
#>      Pinus nigra 2              2           0
#>    Quercus robur 2              1           1
#> # summary() for the share each test flags

The counts match the strict rule on the data frame above. On disk the duplicate test compares each record with all records before it across the files, so it finds record 4 as in the data frame. A rerun into the same directory skips the files already flagged. Large tables on disk covers resuming, duplicates across files and reading the flags back.
